questions.question: What is RSpec and how do you write a spec in it?
questions.title: RSpec Basics
questions.direct_answer: RSpec is a popular, expressive BDD testing framework for Ruby (an alternative to Minitest). A spec describes behavior: `RSpec.describe User do; it 'is valid with a name' do; user = User.new(name: 'Al'); expect(user).to be_valid; end; end`. Expectations: `expect(x).to eq(y)`, `expect(x).to be_truthy`, `expect { ... }.to raise_error(Errno)`, `expect(list).to include(item)`. Setup with `before { ... }` / `let(:user) { User.new(name: 'Al') }` (lazy, memoized). `context 'when admin' do` groups cases; `describe` for grouping. Run with `bundle exec rspec` (or `rspec`). Mocks/stubs: `allow(User).to receive(:find).and_return(user)`. RSpec is more readable (English-like) and feature-rich (matchers, mocks) but an extra dependency and larger than Minitest. Many Rails teams choose RSpec; choose it if you want the expressive DSL and the team is comfortable with it.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overusing mocks/stubs (tests pass but don't test real behavior) — prefer real objects/integration where feasible.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: RSpec: expressive BDD framework. describe/it/expect(x).to eq. let (lazy), before (setup). bundle exec rspec. Alternative to Minitest.

sections.content:
expressive BDD framework. describe/it/expect(x).to eq. let (lazy), before (setup). bundle exec rspec. Alternative to Minitest.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D[describe User] --> I[it 'is valid']
  I --> E[expect(user).to be_valid]
  L[let(:user){...}] --> M[lazy, memoized]
  B[before{...}] --> S[setup]
```

sections.title: RSpec
sections.content:
```ruby
require 'rails_helper'

RSpec.describe User, type: :model do
  let(:user) { User.new(name: 'Al') }      # lazy + memoized per test
  before { ... }                            # setup before each test

  describe 'validations' do
    it 'is valid with a name' do
      expect(user).to be_valid             # matcher (be_valid)
    end

    it 'is invalid without a name' do
      user.name = ''
      expect(user).not_to be_valid
      expect(user.errors[:name]).to include("can't be blank")
    end
  end

  context 'when admin' do                  # groups a case
    let(:user) { User.new(name: 'Al', role: 'admin') }
    it 'can edit' do; expect(user).to be_can_edit; end
  end
end

# Common expectations (matchers):
#   expect(x).to eq(y)            # ==
#   expect(x).to be_truthy / be_falsy
#   expect(x).to be_nil
#   expect(list).to include(item)
#   expect { ... }.to raise_error(Errno::ENOENT)
#   expect(x).to be_valid         # (Rails-specific matcher)
#   expect(x).to receive(:method) # (mock)

# Mocks/stubs:
#   allow(User).to receive(:find).and_return(user)
#   expect(User).to receive(:create).with(name: 'Al')

# Run:
#   bundle exec rspec                       # all specs
#   bundle exec rspec spec/models/user_spec.rb
#   bundle exec rspec spec/models/user_spec.rb:10

# let is lazy (built on first use) + memoized (cached within a test).
# before runs setup; let! runs eagerly (like before).
# context = alias for describe (convention: context 'when ...', describe 'thing').
# RSpec is expressive and feature-rich but an extra dependency; Minitest ships with Ruby.
```

sections.content:
RSpec is a popular, expressive BDD testing framework for Ruby (an alternative to Minitest).

A spec describes behavior: `RSpec.describe User do; it 'is valid with a name' do; user = User.new(name: 'Al'); expect(user).to be_valid; end; end`.

Expectations: `expect(x).to eq(y)`, `expect(x).to be_truthy`, `expect { ... }.to raise_error(Errno)`, `expect(list).to include(item)`. Setup with `before { ... }` / `let(:user) { User.new(name: 'Al') }` (lazy, memoized). `context 'when admin' do` groups cases; `describe` for grouping. Run with `bundle exec rspec` (or `rspec`). Mocks/stubs: `allow(User).to receive(:find).and_return(user)`. RSpec is more readable (English-like) and feature-rich (matchers, mocks) but an extra dependency and larger than Minitest. Many Rails teams choose RSpec; choose it if you want the expressive DSL and the team is comfortable with it.

Overusing mocks/stubs (tests pass but don't test real behavior) — prefer real objects/integration where feasible.

sections.title: RSpec
sections.content:
```ruby
require 'rails_helper'

RSpec.describe User, type: :model do
  let(:user) { User.new(name: 'Al') }      # lazy + memoized per test
  before { ... }                            # setup before each test

  describe 'validations' do
    it 'is valid with a name' do
      expect(user).to be_valid             # matcher (be_valid)
    end

    it 'is invalid without a name' do
      user.name = ''
      expect(user).not_to be_valid
      expect(user.errors[:name]).to include("can't be blank")
    end
  end

  context 'when admin' do                  # groups a case
    let(:user) { User.new(name: 'Al', role: 'admin') }
    it 'can edit' do; expect(user).to be_can_edit; end
  end
end

# Common expectations (matchers):
#   expect(x).to eq(y)            # ==
#   expect(x).to be_truthy / be_falsy
#   expect(x).to be_nil
#   expect(list).to include(item)
#   expect { ... }.to raise_error(Errno::ENOENT)
#   expect(x).to be_valid         # (Rails-specific matcher)
#   expect(x).to receive(:method) # (mock)

# Mocks/stubs:
#   allow(User).to receive(:find).and_return(user)
#   expect(User).to receive(:create).with(name: 'Al')

# Run:
#   bundle exec rspec                       # all specs
#   bundle exec rspec spec/models/user_spec.rb
#   bundle exec rspec spec/models/user_spec.rb:10

# let is lazy (built on first use) + memoized (cached within a test).
# before runs setup; let! runs eagerly (like before).
# context = alias for describe (convention: context 'when ...', describe 'thing').
# RSpec is expressive and feature-rich but an extra dependency; Minitest ships with Ruby.
```
